0.title: Caring for Souls: A Biblical Counseling Guide
0.essay:
This study is a practical guide for pastors, elders, deacons, and any Christian who wants to help others from the word of God. Caring for souls is not a specialist hobby. It is part of the ordinary life of the church.

The tradition behind it

The study draws on the biblical counselling movement, especially the tradition of the Association of Certified Biblical Counselors (ACBC) and its key voices. Jay Adams recovered the conviction that the church is competent to counsel. Randy Patten helped make biblical counselling training widely available. Heath Lambert’s A Theology of Biblical Counseling gives the movement a careful theological foundation. David Powlison’s “X-ray questions” and heart-focused approach shaped a generation. Paul Tripp’s Instruments in the Redeemer’s Hands remains one of the most practical introductions. Steve Viars has shown what a counselling-saturated congregation can look like. Stuart Scott and John Street have championed medical referral and the counselling of men. Martha Peace and Amy Baker have served women with wisdom and care. And Brad Bigney’s Gospel Treason makes the diagnosis of idols accessible.

Four movements

The study has four parts. Foundations (chapters 1–5): why Scripture is sufficient, how to understand the whole person, how to distinguish sin and suffering, how to reach the heart, and how to listen and speak. Common struggles (chapters 6–10): anxiety, depression, anger, grief and loss, and burnout. Hard cases (chapters 11–20): sexual addiction, eating disorders, alcohol and drugs, gambling, severe mental illness, OCD and intrusive thoughts, trauma and sexual abuse, suicide and self-harm, domestic abuse, and Alzheimer’s and other dementias. And finally, recommended literature (chapter 21) to take you further.

Two convictions

Two convictions run through everything. The first is the sufficiency of Scripture. “All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:16–17). God’s divine power “has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness” (2 Peter 1:3).

The second is the medical principle, stressed by Street, Scott and the ACBC tradition: always refer for a medical check-up, because the body matters and physical causes must be ruled out. But refer and counsel at the same time. Do not wait. The soul needs the word on the same day the body needs the doctor.

The goal

The goal of biblical counselling is not symptom management, or even simply restored functioning. It is the glory of God: that the person in front of you would come to know God more truly, trust Christ more deeply and live in ways that honour him. Every step and every hard conversation serves this: that they would flourish as a creature made for God, redeemed for his glory, and being conformed to the image of his Son.

For reflection

Who in your church, or your life, is quietly struggling and needs someone to come alongside them with the word of God?

1.title: Foundations: The Sufficiency of Scripture
1.essay:
Every approach to counselling rests on assumptions about what is wrong with human beings and what can make them well. Biblical counselling begins with the conviction that God’s word is sufficient for the care of souls.

Two diagnoses

Secular psychology generally assumes that our deepest problems are psychological, rooted in developmental history, neurological patterns or environmental conditioning, and that the solution lies in insight, relearning or medication. Biblical counselling does not dismiss the body or deny that our history shapes us. But it insists that our deepest problem is always spiritual — a disordered heart, disordered worship, disordered relationships with God and others — and that the deepest remedy is the word and Spirit of God.

The church reclaims its task

Before the 1970s, most seminaries trained pastors to preach but sent people with emotional and relational struggles to secular therapists. The ancient pastoral “cure of souls” had largely been surrendered. Jay Adams’s Competent to Counsel (1970) was controversial but necessary: the church had the resources all along.

The movement has matured since Adams. Powlison, Tripp, Lambert and Edward Welch have developed a richer, more pastorally sensitive approach that takes suffering seriously and refuses to reduce every problem to simple sin. But the foundation has not shifted: Scripture is sufficient.

What sufficiency means

Heath Lambert puts it precisely: the Bible contains everything necessary for the counsellor to understand people accurately, to diagnose their problems accurately, and to point them to real and lasting change. That is not because the Bible answers every technical question in psychiatry. It is because it reveals the God who made the human heart and who alone can heal it.

“His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence” (2 Peter 1:3). God has not left his people without what they need to know him, understand themselves and walk in his ways. So a counsellor who believes this will reach for Scripture first, not because they are against science, but because they know where ultimate wisdom lies.

What sufficiency does not mean

It does not mean the counsellor knows everything, or that medical care is unnecessary, or that every problem has a simple spiritual answer. It means Scripture provides the framework — the map of the human person, the diagnosis of the fundamental problem, and the direction of true healing — within which all other knowledge, medical, relational or historical, finds its proper place.

Secular psychology can make useful observations about human behaviour. But it cannot diagnose the heart before God, cannot atone for sin, and cannot produce the new birth that is the only foundation of lasting change. An approach that mixes secular frameworks with Scripture as equal authorities compromises sufficiency at its root.

Four uses of Scripture

Paul names four uses of Scripture that map directly onto counselling: “teaching,” bringing true biblical categories; “reproof,” showing honestly and lovingly where someone has gone wrong; “correction,” pointing the way back through repentance; and “training in righteousness,” the long work of forming new habits and character (2 Timothy 3:16). And the goal is not symptom relief but a person who is “complete, equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:17).

A living word

“For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12). The counsellor’s primary tool is not a static text but a living one. It does things in people as it is heard. It cuts to exactly the depth required, reaching not just behaviour but motive. No questionnaire does that. The counsellor who brings Scripture is not offering their own insight, but a sword the Spirit wields with perfect knowledge of the heart.

Able to instruct one another

Paul writes, “I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another” (Romans 15:14). The word for instruct gave Adams the name “nouthetic counselling.” And notice to whom Paul says it: not to professional therapists, but to a whole congregation. Biblical counselling is not a specialist guild. It is the calling of the church. Every member of a healthy church should be growing in the ability to speak truth into a struggling person’s life with competence and care.

The subtler temptation

The temptation today is rarely to abandon Scripture outright. It is to dilute it: to add secular frameworks as supplements, to make psychological language the primary vocabulary for diagnosis, and to treat the Bible as devotional encouragement rather than the sharp, living instrument it is. The biblical counsellor holds the line, not out of defensiveness, but out of conviction. God’s word is enough, and in the hands of the Spirit it is more than enough.

For reflection

When someone brings you a problem, what do you reach for first? What would it look like to trust that Scripture is truly sufficient for the struggles you meet?

2.title: Understanding People: The Biblical Anatomy of the Soul
2.essay:
Before you can counsel anyone, you need to understand them, not just their presenting problem but who they are. Biblical counselling begins with a rich account of the person.

The whole person

Every person you counsel is made in God’s image, fallen in Adam, redeemable in Christ, and, if a believer, indwelt by the Spirit. They live in a body, are shaped by a history, are woven into relationships, and live in a world that both blesses and afflicts them. Scripture speaks of heart, soul, mind, strength, spirit and body, not as separate compartments but as dimensions of one unified person.

This person, this situation

David Powlison insisted that counselling must engage the specifics of a life: not generic categories, but this person, in this situation, with this history, these relationships and these patterns of thought, desire and behaviour. Paul Tripp adds the language of story. Everyone is living inside a story about who they are, what they need and how the world works. Often that story has been shaped more by painful experience than by Scripture. The counsellor helps them see their story within the larger, truer story of creation, redemption and new creation.

So resist the temptation to categorise someone before you have understood them. Tripp’s “know” step means taking time to understand a person’s history, relationships, losses and joys before making any diagnosis. The counsellor who listens well in the first hour will speak far more accurately in the second.

The heart is the source

“Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23). In Scripture, the heart is the control centre of the person: it thinks, desires, chooses and worships. Everything else flows from it. Address behaviour without the heart and you get behaviour modification. Address the heart, and genuine transformation becomes possible.

Jesus overturned the assumption that sin is mainly external: “For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person” (Mark 7:21–23).

That diagnosis is both humbling and hopeful. Humbling, because no change of environment, medication or willpower reaches the root. Hopeful, because God promises the one thing that truly matters: “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).

Worshippers

Every person is worshipping something at every moment. The question is what. Part of the counsellor’s task is to help identify what the heart is really worshipping, and to redirect that worship to the only One worthy of it.

Dignity and fallenness

The person before you bears the image of God. They have dignity, rationality, moral capacity and relational depth no secular framework fully explains. And they are fallen. Every faculty is affected by sin: the mind thinks crookedly, the will chooses poorly, emotions respond out of proportion, the body suffers. Both truths must be held together, without collapsing into either despair or naivety.

The body matters

Paul prays, “may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Scripture refuses both to spiritualise away the physical and to reduce the spiritual to the physical.

Edward Welch has helped the movement here. Sleep deprivation, chronic illness, hormonal change and neurological conditions all affect how a person thinks, feels and functions. That is no excuse for sin, but it is a real context. Someone who has not slept properly for weeks, or who is managing a chronic illness, deserves a counsellor who sees body and soul together, as God made them.

Welch’s Running Scared and Shame Interrupted show the richness of this approach. Rather than labelling anxiety simply as sinful distrust, he explores the many dimensions of fear: legitimate fears, distorted fears, and fears that are sinful and deserve sympathy at the same time. That nuance has made him a trusted guide for sufferers who have been handled too roughly by less careful counsellors.

Flesh and Spirit

“For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do” (Galatians 5:17). This conflict is not between body and soul, but between the old self and the new. Every believer lives in that tension.

Understanding it guards against two errors: the moralist, who expects simple obedience once the right principle is named, and the therapist, who expects the person to feel better once they are understood. Change is neither simple nor merely felt. It is the Spirit’s work through the word, in community, over time.

For reflection

Think of someone you are trying to help. How much do you really know of their story, their body, their relationships and their heart? What questions do you still need to ask?

3.title: Sin, Suffering, and Sanctification
3.essay:
One of the most important skills in counselling is the ability to tell sin and suffering apart, and then to hold them together in the right relationship.

Two failures

Many counselling failures come from getting this wrong. Treating every problem as sin crushes suffering people under guilt they do not deserve. Treating every problem as suffering removes appropriate responsibility and leaves people stuck.

Powlison’s framework helps. Some people come primarily as sufferers: they have been sinned against, afflicted by disease, crushed by loss. Others come primarily as sinners, reaping what they have sown. Most come as both: they have suffered in ways they did not choose, and responded in ways that are sinful. The counsellor must discern which is primary in this moment, without ignoring the other.

Not always punishment

When the disciples assumed a man’s blindness was punishment for sin, Jesus corrected them: “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him” (John 9:3). The counsellor must hold this before every sufferer. Not every affliction is the consequence of your own sin. Some suffering is the setting in which God means to display his power and faithfulness.

A person grieving the death of a child does not need to be told their grief is sinful. They need the “God of all comfort” (2 Corinthians 1:3). But a person whose marriage has broken down because of their own choices needs more than sympathy. They need honest, loving confrontation alongside it.

Count it joy

“Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness” (James 1:2–3). James does not say feel joy, but count it joy: a choice of interpretation. The trial is real and painful, and the joy is not denial but faith’s reframing. For the believer, suffering is not pointless. God is working in it to produce something ease never could. The counsellor holds this out not as a cliché, but as a conviction that shapes how suffering is endured.

Suffering processed with God

“We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame” (Romans 5:3–5). That chain is not automatic. It describes suffering processed with God, by faith, in community. Suffering that is numbed, denied or carried alone does not usually bear this fruit. The counsellor walks with the sufferer into the suffering, not around it, trusting that God is at work in the very pain they most want to escape.

Two kinds of sorrow

“For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). Godly grief faces sin honestly, feels its weight, and moves towards God with it. Worldly grief — guilt, self-loathing, despair — faces the sin but moves away from God, sinking into self-condemnation with no resolution. The counsellor helps people move from one to the other, not by minimising their sin, but by pointing to the God who receives penitents with open arms.

Order matters

Picture a woman who was abused as a child and now struggles with deep shame and distorted thinking about God. A careless counsellor might focus at once on her sinful responses, her bitterness or wrong beliefs. A wiser counsellor spends a long time first acknowledging the suffering: hearing the pain, lamenting what was done to her. Only later, gently and over time, do they help her see where her own responses have become sinful patterns. Both were true. The order mattered enormously.

Sanctification as the goal

Steve Viars stresses that biblical counselling is not crisis management. It is discipleship. The aim is not to return someone to how they were before the crisis, but to see them more fully conformed to Christ through it. That gives every counselling relationship a forward direction: not only “What happened to you?” but “Who is God calling you to be through this?”

Neither sin nor suffering is the last word. Christ is the last word, and he is making his people like himself through both.

Before each conversation

Ask yourself: is this primarily a sin issue, a suffering issue, or both? What does this person most need from me today: honest confrontation, compassionate presence, or both? Let the answer shape how you open, which Scriptures you bring, and how much you speak or listen.

For reflection

Do you tend to treat problems more as sin or more as suffering? Think of someone you are helping: what do they most need from you right now?

4.title: The Heart: Where Counseling Actually Happens
4.essay:
Biblical counselling’s central category is the heart. Every presenting problem — conflict, addiction, anxiety, depression, relational breakdown — has a heart dimension, and the counsellor who addresses only behaviour will see temporary change at best.

The control centre

In Scripture the heart is not mainly the seat of emotion, as in modern usage. It is the inner person: the place of thought, desire, will and worship, the source from which all behaviour flows.

X-ray questions

David Powlison developed what he called X-ray questions: careful, prayerful questions designed to surface what is happening in the heart beneath the presenting problem. They include questions like these. What do you want most in this situation? What do you fear most? What would make you feel that life is good? What are you trusting to give you that? What would you be willing to sin to get, or to keep? Whose approval matters most to you? What does this situation say about you, and why does that matter so much?

Asked with genuine care, these are not accusations. They help the counselee see their own heart more clearly, and they show the counsellor which Scripture to bring to which heart issue.

Where quarrels come from

“What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel” (James 4:1–2). The quarrelling person thinks the problem is what the other person did. James says: look inside. You want something so badly that when you do not get it, you fight for it. The idol beneath the conflict is whatever you are willing to damage relationships to obtain or protect.

Treasure and heart

“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). What a person pours their resources, attention, energy and emotion into is what controls them, their functional god. That is why the X-ray questions circle around what matters most and what they fear losing. And the gospel’s invitation is breathtaking: there is a treasure worth staking everything on, “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading” (1 Peter 1:4).

A factory of idols

Calvin described the human mind as a perpetual factory of idols. Brad Bigney’s Gospel Treason makes this diagnosis practical. When anything other than God becomes what we must have to be all right — when our sense of worth, safety, love or control depends on someone or something else — we have committed idolatry. And idolatry always produces misery, because the idol cannot deliver what it promises, and its worship deforms the worshipper.

Keller, Tripp and Powlison all see idolatry beneath most presenting problems. The angry person is often worshipping something they believe they must have. The anxious person is trusting something other than God for security. The depressed person may be worshipping an approval or achievement they have lost or can never reach. The counsellor’s task is not to shame them for this, but to expose it gently and redirect the heart to the only One who truly satisfies.

The gospel is the answer

The answer to idolatry is not willpower or behaviour modification. It is the gospel: the news that God has given in Christ everything the heart has been seeking from its idols. Security, acceptance, love, significance and purpose are all found in Christ, freely, without performance. The counsellor who keeps bringing people back to the cross — to what God has already done and given — is doing the most important work of all.

Picture a man whose anger at his wife is rooted in a craving for respect. He needs it so desperately that any perceived slight triggers rage. Once that idol is named, the gospel can speak to it: in Christ, you are already fully honoured and valued by the One whose opinion ultimately matters. His anger will not vanish overnight. But the direction of change becomes clear. He is not just trying to be less angry; he is learning to trust Christ for what he had been demanding from his wife.

God changes hearts

“And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). The most important thing a counsellor must know is that heart change is God’s work, not theirs. We speak, listen, question, encourage and rebuke. Only God removes the heart of stone.

That is the counsellor’s greatest comfort and greatest humility. You are not the agent of change. You are the instrument. The Spirit uses the word through human relationship to do what only he can do. A counsellor who understands this will pray more than they strategise, and trust the Spirit’s work even when they cannot see it.

Try one question

In your next conversation, after you have listened carefully, try one X-ray question: “What do you want most in this situation?” Then listen. Whatever comes out — safety, control, respect, love, vindication, relief — is the beginning of a heart diagnosis. From there you can bring the gospel specifically: Christ offers you exactly this, fully and freely, now.

For reflection

Apply the X-ray questions to yourself. What do you want most right now? What do you fear losing? What might that reveal about your own heart’s worship?

5.title: Listening and Speaking: The Practice of Gospel Conversation
5.essay:
Biblical counselling is a conversation: one conducted in prayer, shaped by Scripture and aimed at a person’s transformation by the grace of God. And the first rule of that conversation is to listen before you speak.

Love, know, speak, do

Paul Tripp’s Instruments in the Redeemer’s Hands describes four movements. Love: build a genuine relationship. Know: understand the person’s story by listening carefully. Speak: bring the word to bear with truth and grace. Do: follow through with practical steps and accountability.

Most counsellors jump to “speak” before they have adequately “known.” The result is accurate theology delivered to the wrong person at the wrong time.

Folly and shame

“If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame” (Proverbs 18:13). This may be the most practically important verse for counsellors. The temptation to answer before truly hearing is almost universal. We hear a problem that resembles one we have met before, and we reach for the familiar verse or advice.

The discipline of truly hearing — asking follow-up questions, reflecting back what you heard, resisting the urge to speak until you understand — is among the hardest skills to develop and among the most important. A person who feels truly heard is far more open to truth. A person who feels processed has already closed up. The counsellor who can repeat back what someone has said in a way that makes them feel understood has earned the right to speak.

The ministry of presence

When Job’s friends first came, “they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great” (Job 2:13). That was their finest hour, before they opened their mouths. They did not explain, minimise or theologise. They came and stayed. The ministry of presence is itself a form of counsel, and in the early stages of a crisis, often the most important one.

Warning and teaching

Paul describes his own ministry: “Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ” (Colossians 1:28). It is Christ-centred, it is for everyone, and it goes in two directions: warning and teaching. Warning without teaching becomes legalism. Teaching without warning becomes sentimentality. And the goal is not merely resolved problems but mature people.

Truth in love

“Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ” (Ephesians 4:15). Truth without love becomes a weapon: accurate, precise and wounding without healing. Love without truth becomes a deception: comfortable and affirming, but leaving the person without direction. The goal of speaking is always growth into Christ, not the counsellor’s satisfaction at having said the right thing.

The shape of a session

A simple pattern helps. Open with prayer, declaring dependence on the Spirit rather than your own wisdom. Listen carefully, letting the person tell their story. Clarify and reflect back, showing you have understood. Ask a diagnostic question to surface the heart issue gently. Bring one well-chosen Scripture that speaks to it. Discuss together how it applies. Agree a practical step before you next meet. And close with prayer, bringing everything before God together.

Homework

Randy Patten and the ACBC tradition stress homework, not as busywork but as the bridge between the conversation and real life. It should be specific — not “read your Bible more,” but “read Philippians 4:6–9 each morning, and write down one thing you are anxious about and one thing you can thank God for.” It should be achievable, and it should be reviewed next time. Without accountability, insight rarely becomes change.

The church as the setting

Steve Viars adds that counselling does not happen in a vacuum. It belongs within the life of the church: the congregation that worships, prays and serves together. A counsellor who connects someone to genuine community is offering more than technique. They are offering the setting in which lasting change happens.

Martha Peace and Amy Baker have shown the particular value of women counselling women. The issues many women bring — shame, body image, relational wounds, abuse, and the struggles of marriage and motherhood — are often best addressed by an older woman who has walked similar roads and can speak with both authority and understanding. A church that equips trained women counsellors alongside its pastors is far better able to care for the whole body.

Keep learning

After your next counselling conversation, ask honestly: how much did I speak, and how much did I listen? Did I bring Scripture too early, or at the right moment? Did we agree a next step? Did I pray? These questions are not for guilt but for growth.

For reflection

When did you last feel truly heard by someone? What did they do? How could you offer that same kind of listening to someone this week?

6.title: Common Struggles: Anxiety
6.essay:
Anxiety is the most common struggle brought to pastors and counsellors, and one of the most often mishandled.

Two errors

On one side is the moraliser, who quickly quotes Philippians 4:6 and tells the anxious person to stop worrying because God is in control. The theology is accurate, but delivered without understanding, it leaves the person ashamed of something they already know they should not feel. On the other side is the therapist who validates the anxiety and teaches coping strategies, but never addresses the heart beneath it. Biblical counselling seeks a third way: compassionate, patient, truth-filled engagement with the particular heart issues driving this person’s anxiety.

Many kinds of fear

Edward Welch’s Running Scared is one of the most helpful treatments. Anxiety is not simply sinful distrust. It is often a mixture of legitimate fear (we live in a genuinely dangerous world), distorted fear (threats magnified beyond reality), and functional unbelief (trusting something other than God for safety). A counsellor who rebukes only the sinful part, without acknowledging the legitimate part, will not help, and may harm.

See a doctor, and begin now

Some anxiety has physical contributors: thyroid problems, hormonal changes, stimulant use, sleep deprivation and other conditions. Refer for a medical check-up straight away. But do not wait for the results before beginning to counsel. Body and soul need attention at the same time.

Finding the heart of it

Before bringing Scripture, ask questions that surface the heart beneath the anxiety. What specifically are you most afraid will happen? What would that mean about you, or your life? What are you trying to control, and why does losing control feel so threatening? If the worst happened, what would you lose? Is there something or someone you are trusting more than God to keep you safe? What does your anxiety say about what you believe God is like?

These are invitations, not interrogations. Listen carefully. The answers will show you which Scripture to bring, and how.

Prayer instead of worry

“Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:6–7).

Notice the structure. The alternative to anxiety is not the resolution of the problem, but prayer. Paul does not say everything will work out. He says: bring your anxiety to God, specifically and with thanksgiving, and his peace will stand guard over your heart. It is not a technique but a relationship. The anxious person is invited not to stop feeling, but to turn their feelings towards the Father who can receive them. And the peace that follows is God’s gift, not their achievement, which is exactly why it surpasses understanding.

Of more value

Jesus said, “Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?” (Matthew 6:26). His argument is not that our problems are unreal. It is a question about value. At root, anxiety often asks whether God is attentive, and whether he values us enough to be trusted with the thing we fear losing. Jesus’ answer is a Father who notices sparrows, counts hairs, and values his children beyond calculation.

Functional unbelief

Chronic anxiety often reflects a belief, not stated but functionally held, that God is not attentive enough, powerful enough or good enough to be trusted with what we most fear. That is less a character flaw than a spiritual wound, and the gospel speaks directly to it. The counsellor’s task is to help the person experience, not just agree with, the truth about God as Father, Sovereign and Redeemer.

Peter writes, “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). The word cast is strong: a deliberate throwing. And the reason is personal: he cares for you. Not a generic concern for humanity, but specific care for this person. Made personal and prayed specifically, this verse can be one of the most powerful tools a counsellor has.

In the storm

When the disciples were caught in a storm on the lake, their fear was understandable; the storm was real. In Mark’s account, Jesus first rebuked the wind — “Peace! Be still!” — and then turned to their hearts: “Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?” (Mark 4:39–40). He addressed the reality first, then the heart.

The anxious person often needs the counsellor to slow down with them before speeding up to solutions. Sit in the storm with them first. Hear what they fear. Then, gently and specifically, introduce the God who is bigger than the storm, and who is already in the boat with them.

The goal: trust

The goal of counselling anxiety is not merely a calmer person, though that is a welcome by-product. It is a person who increasingly glorifies God by trusting him: in the dark, in uncertainty, in real danger. Every choice of prayer over rumination, gratitude over dread, and trust over control is an act of worship. A good first step: each day this week, write down one specific fear and one specific truth about God that speaks to it, and bring both to him in prayer.

For reflection

What are you most anxious about right now? What does that anxiety suggest you believe about God? Which promise of his speaks most directly to it?

7.title: Common Struggles: Depression
7.essay:
Depression is one of the most complex and important struggles a counsellor will meet. It is neither simply sinful unbelief nor simply a matter of brain chemistry.

Many dimensions

Heath Lambert’s A Theology of Biblical Counseling and Edward Welch’s Depression: A Stubborn Darkness are essential guides, and both start in the same place. Depression usually involves physical, relational, circumstantial and spiritual dimensions at once, and the wise counsellor attends to all of them.

Sufficiency of Scripture does not mean depression has a simple spiritual answer. It means Scripture gives the framework for engaging every dimension: the physical (God made the body, and it matters), the relational (isolation makes depression worse, and community is prescribed), and the spiritual (what is this person believing about God, themselves and their future?).

See a doctor, and begin now

Depression can have medical contributors: thyroid problems, vitamin deficiencies, hormonal changes, sleep disorders and more. Refer for a full medical check-up immediately, and begin counselling at the same time. And if there is any sign of suicidal thinking, turn to the chapter on suicide and self-harm and follow emergency steps at once.

Elijah under the broom tree

The Bible’s most detailed case study is Elijah. After the triumph on Mount Carmel, threatened by Jezebel, he fled into the wilderness, sat under a broom tree and prayed, “It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life” (1 Kings 19:4).

God’s first response was not a sermon but a meal. He let the exhausted prophet sleep, and then an angel touched him and said, “Arise and eat” (1 Kings 19:5). He slept again, and the angel came a second time: “Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you” (1 Kings 19:7). Food, rest, gentle questions, presence, and only then a renewed commission.

The order matters. God did not rebuke Elijah before caring for his body. A depressed person who is not sleeping, eating or leaving the house needs those physical realities addressed alongside the spiritual ones, not after them. The counsellor who asks, “Are you sleeping? Are you eating? Are you getting outside?” is not avoiding the spiritual. They are honouring the connection God built between body and soul.

Questions to ask

When did you first notice this? Was there a specific loss, disappointment or change before it began? What has changed about how you see yourself? How do you see God right now — near or distant, good or indifferent? What do you believe about your future? Are there thoughts that keep recurring? When did you last spend time with someone who loves you? Depression often has layers — grief, loss, distorted beliefs, spiritual dryness, physical neglect — and you need to understand which are present before you know which truth to bring.

Preaching to yourself

The psalmist does something remarkable: “Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him” (Psalm 42:5). He does not suppress the darkness; he names it and faces it. Nor does he surrender to it; he commands his soul towards truth. That double movement — honest acknowledgment and deliberate hope — is the biblical pattern. The counsellor models it by taking the depth of the person’s experience seriously without staying there, and by gently, persistently pointing to the God who is the true source of hope.

Sin and suffering

Some depression is closely tied to sinful patterns: unconfessed sin, unresolved bitterness, persistent withdrawal. That must be addressed honestly. But much depression is primarily suffering, the fruit of loss, illness or being sinned against. A counsellor who only rebukes never helps; one who only sympathises never moves the person forward. Wisdom judges the proportion of truth and compassion needed at each moment.

Spurgeon

Charles Spurgeon, perhaps the greatest preacher of the nineteenth century, struggled with depression throughout his ministry, and was at times laid aside for long periods. He wrote and preached honestly about it, and his people loved him more for it. A pastor who has walked through darkness and found God faithful there can say from the inside what the psalmist says: I shall again praise him.

One truth, well placed

When you sit with someone in depression, resist the urge to fix things quickly. A person who has been in darkness for weeks or months needs you to sit with them for a while before you speak. Ask the questions. Listen to the whole story. Then bring one truth that speaks specifically to what you have heard. A single well-placed truth is worth more than a dozen general encouragements offered too soon.

The goal: trusting God in the valley

The goal is not simply feeling better, but honouring God in the darkness: not only “When will this end?” but “How can I trust God here, today?” A person who learns to pray honestly in depression, to receive care from others, and to hold on to truth when they cannot feel it, glorifies God in a way that ease never could. A simple next step: each day this week, write one honest lament, in the spirit of Psalm 88, and then read a promise of God’s presence such as Isaiah 43:2.

For reflection

Is there someone you know who is in a “broom tree” season? What would it look like to care for their body as well as their soul, as God cared for Elijah?

8.title: Common Struggles: Anger
8.essay:
Anger is one of the most common and destructive problems in counselling, appearing in marriages, families, workplaces and churches with painful regularity. Beneath most sinful anger lies an unmet demand.

Not all anger is sinful

God is angry at evil: he is “a God who feels indignation every day” (Psalm 7:11). Jesus “looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart” (Mark 3:5). Righteous anger — anger at genuine sin and injustice, proportionate to the offence, held without vengeance — is not only permitted but sometimes required.

But most of the anger brought to counselling is not this. It is the anger of a heart that worships comfort, respect, control or approval, and punishes whoever threatens the idol. The counsellor helps the person make the distinction: is this righteous anger, or idolatry in motion?

See a doctor, and begin now

Rage and irritability can be linked to hormonal problems, sleep disorders or neurological conditions. Refer for a medical check-up, and begin counselling at the same time.

Questions to ask

What specifically triggered the anger? What did you want in that moment that you did not get, or what did you fear losing? What did you believe the other person owed you? Honestly, was there a sense of entitlement? What did the anger feel like it was protecting? What does this pattern say about what matters most to you?

Stuart Scott traces most sinful anger to pride: the belief that I deserve better, know better, or should have more say than I am getting. Name the idol beneath the anger, gently and clearly.

Where fights come from

“What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?” (James 4:1). The angry person thinks the problem is what the other person did. James says: look inside. The counsellor does not excuse the other person, who may have done real wrong. But they help the angry person see that their response reveals something deeper than the trigger. Addressing only the trigger produces temporary restraint at best.

Quick to hear

“Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:19–20). That is the exact reverse of the angry person’s instinct: slow to hear, quick to speak, quick to anger. Overriding it takes both the Spirit’s work and deliberate practice. A practical plan for the next provocation might be: stop, breathe, ask a question, and pray silently before responding. Heart change without new habits is incomplete, just as new habits without heart change are mere behaviour management.

Before the sun goes down

“Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil” (Ephesians 4:26–27). Paul acknowledges that anger comes, but forbids making it a home. The boundary is time. Unresolved anger nursed overnight becomes bitterness, resentment, and finally the hardened contempt that destroys relationships.

Humility is the medicine

If pride is the root, humility is the cure: a true estimate of oneself before God. “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5). The humble person is not easily provoked, because they are not constantly measuring whether others are giving them what they deserve. They have already placed themselves at God’s mercy and received far more than they could ask. From there, other people’s failures shrink to their proper size.

Cain

Cain’s anger is the Bible’s first portrait of sinful anger. God came to him with a question: “Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?” (Genesis 4:6). Then a warning: “sin is crouching at the door” (Genesis 4:7). The warning came before the act. Tragically, Cain did not heed it.

God’s question is the counsellor’s first question too. Many angry people have never been asked what they want in the moment they explode. The anger feels like a reflex, not a choice. Slow, caring, specific questions often bring a moment of real surprise: “I’ve never thought of it like that.” That moment of insight is not the end of the work, but it is a necessary beginning.

The goal: transformed anger

The goal is not the absence of all anger, but its transformation: from the hot, fast, self-serving anger of the idol-worshipper to the slow, measured, justice-seeking anger of someone who has entrusted their cause to God. “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). It is a long road of daily repentance and growing humility. Each conquered outburst is an act of worship. A useful exercise: after each angry episode this week, write down what triggered it, what you wanted, and one truth about God that speaks to that want.

For reflection

Think of the last time you were angry. What did you want that you were not getting? What might that reveal about your heart?

9.title: Common Struggles: Grief and Loss
9.essay:
Grief is one of the most natural and necessary human experiences, and one of the most poorly handled in Christian communities.

Too quick to comfort

The impulse to comfort quickly, to point to resurrection hope before the tears have been shed, to say “they’re in a better place” before the person has had space to feel the loss, is well-meaning but often harmful. Grief is not a spiritual deficiency. It is the right response of a heart formed by love to the loss of someone or something truly loved.

The goal is not to move people through grief quickly, but to help them grieve with God: bringing the full weight of the loss into his presence through lament, finding that he can bear it, and slowly, over time, finding that he is rebuilding what has been broken.

Jesus wept

“Jesus wept” (John 11:35). He knew he was about to raise Lazarus. He knew the story would end well. He wept anyway, because Mary was weeping, because death is genuinely terrible, and because he entered fully into human loss rather than standing above it.

That is the counsellor’s model. Do not skip to the resurrection before sitting in the tomb. The person who is weeping needs someone to weep with them first. The truth of resurrection, glorious as it is, lands far deeper in a heart that has first been given room to feel the loss.

The shape of the grief

Grief takes many shapes. Ask: What have you lost? (They may not have named it clearly yet.) How long ago? What did this person or thing mean in your life? Are you angry as well as sad, and at whom? Are you angry at God? What do you believe God is doing in this, or do you feel he has abandoned you? Is there guilt mixed in, something you wish you had said or done? Are you sleeping, eating, and spending time with people who love you? A counsellor who understands the specific shape of the grief can bring Scripture that truly speaks, rather than general comfort that lands nowhere.

A psalm for the darkest night

Psalm 88 is the darkest psalm, and it ends without resolution. The psalmist says, “For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol” (Psalm 88:3), and the last words are “my companions have become darkness” (Psalm 88:18). God put it in the Bible. So even absolute despair is within the scope of prayer and within the community of faith. A counsellor who can say honestly, “This psalm was written for moments like yours,” gives the gift of being understood by God himself.

Lament as discipline

About a third of the psalms are laments. A church that does not know how to lament, that moves too quickly from tragedy to triumph, does not reflect the full range of biblical spirituality. Teaching people to bring their unfiltered pain to God, rather than suppressing it or dressing it in premature hope, is teaching one of the deepest forms of prayer.

Lamentations, the Bible’s long meditation on grief, is raw and honest and sometimes angry. Yet in its very middle comes this: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases” (Lamentations 3:22). That truth is not where grief begins. It is found in the middle of it, held on to with both hands in the dark.

Not as those without hope

Paul writes “that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Notice: he does not say we do not grieve. Resurrection hope does not bypass grief; it shapes it. It gives grief a horizon. The loss is real, the sorrow is real, and the love behind it was real. And one day the One who makes all things new will “wipe away every tear” (Revelation 21:4). The counsellor holds that hope out gently, at the right time, not as an escape from the pain, but as its final answer.

David and Absalom

When David heard that his rebellious son had been killed, he cried, “O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!” (2 Samuel 18:33). It is one of the rawest expressions of a parent’s grief in all literature, from a man after God’s own heart. Grief does not indicate weak faith. It indicates deep love.

Listen without fixing

The most important thing you can do in early conversations with a grieving person is listen without fixing. Say, “Tell me about them. Tell me what you loved most. Tell me what you miss.” Let the tears come. You will earn far more trust with “Tell me more” than with “They’re in a better place” in the first five minutes.

The goal: honest grief

The goal is not the end of sorrow but grief that glorifies God: honest enough to bring real pain into his presence, trusting enough to believe he can bear it, and hopeful enough to cling to his promises when they cannot be felt. It is the faith of Job: “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (Job 13:15). A gentle next step is to read a psalm of lament, such as Psalm 42, 77 or 88, and write a short, honest prayer in the same spirit.

For reflection

When others grieve, are you more likely to comfort quickly or to sit with them? What loss in your own life still needs to be brought honestly to God?

10.title: Common Struggles: Burnout
10.essay:
Burnout — chronic exhaustion, cynicism and declining effectiveness after long periods of high demand — is not a modern invention. Scripture shows it in some of its most faithful servants.

Biblical portraits

Elijah collapsed under the broom tree (1 Kings 19). Moses, overwhelmed by the people’s complaints, cried, “I am not able to carry all this people alone; the burden is too heavy for me” (Numbers 11:14). Martha “was distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:40).

Burnout appears most often in those who care most: pastors, counsellors, nurses, teachers, carers, parents of demanding children, and anyone who has given more than they could sustain for a long time. It is both physical and spiritual, and both must be addressed.

Empty, not lazy

Burnout overlaps with depression but is not the same. The burned-out person is often less sad than empty: hollowed out, with nothing left to give. The detachment, the cynicism, the sense that nothing makes a difference, are protective mechanisms, the soul’s attempt to stop the bleeding. Understanding this helps the counsellor come with compassion rather than rebuke. This person is not lazy. They are depleted.

See a doctor, and begin now

Burnout can overlap with thyroid problems, anaemia, sleep disorders and depression with physical components. Refer for a medical check-up, and begin counselling alongside it.

The heart beneath the exhaustion

The heart questions matter. Often the burned-out person has been driven by something other than love for God: the need for approval, an idol of productivity, an inability to receive help, or the belief that their worth depends on their usefulness. A counsellor who addresses only the exhaustion will see them return to the same pattern once they have recovered enough to start again.

So ask: How long have you felt this way? When did you start giving more than you could sustain, and what drove that? What would have happened if you had said no? Whose approval were you trying to secure? Is it easy or hard for you to receive help? Does rest feel safe, or like failure? Do you feel your worth is tied to your usefulness? What do you think God thinks of you when you are not productive? The answers often surface the idol, and naming it opens the door to grace.

The journey is too great

God’s response to Elijah is the Bible’s most instructive passage on burnout. No rebuke, no lecture on trust. Just sleep, food and an angel’s touch: “Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you” (1 Kings 19:7). God acknowledged the weight before he prescribed anything. A counsellor who attends first to sleep, food and basic rhythms before pressing into heart work is following God’s own pattern.

An easy yoke

“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30).

The burned-out person is often carrying a yoke Jesus never placed on them: earning worth through performance, justifying their existence through usefulness, securing love through output. His invitation is radical: come and receive. It is not the end of work, for his yoke is still a yoke. But it is work from rest, not work for rest.

Rest as trust

“For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day” (Exodus 20:11). God rested not from weariness, but because the work was complete. The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, who is our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the rhythm of work and rest remains God’s gift. It calls us back to creaturely dependence. You are not the sustainer of the universe. You never were. Rest, and let God be God.

A person who cannot rest has not yet fully believed that God is God and they are not, that the world will not stop turning if they stop working. Rest is not laziness. It is worship and trust.

Sharing the load

God’s answer to Moses was structural: seventy elders to share the burden (Numbers 11:16–17). His response to unsustainable burdens is often a redistribution of responsibility and an honest naming of the limits he has placed on every finite creature. The burned-out person often needs not only rest but restructuring: what is God calling me to stop doing, so that someone else can do it?

Martha, Martha

Martha, busy and resentful, complained that her sister was not helping. Jesus said gently, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion” (Luke 10:41–42). It was not a rebuke of service, but an invitation to priority. The burned-out person has usually lost the discipline of sitting at Jesus’ feet: receiving, being still. Recovery begins there.

Churches that rest

Burnout in ministry is common, and the church must name it honestly. A pastor running on empty cannot give what they do not have. A congregation that truly loves its leaders will build in structures for rest, cover seasons of recovery without shame, and receive the Lord’s Day as a shared gift of rest and worship.

The goal: new rhythms

The goal is not only recovery but a restructured life. A practical first step: identify one specific thing to stop doing this week. Not postpone, but stop. Then notice what it costs you emotionally, and what that reveals about your heart.

For reflection

Are you carrying a yoke Jesus never placed on you? What is one thing you need to stop doing, so that you can sit at his feet?

11.title: Hard Cases: Sexual Addiction and Pornography
11.essay:
Pornography addiction is one of the most common struggles brought to pastors today, and one of the least spoken about. The person who finally discloses it has usually carried the secret for years, and is drowning in shame.

Neither shocked nor minimising

The pastoral failures here are disgust, or moralistic pressure to “just stop,” which the person has already applied to themselves a thousand times without success. Neither works. What is needed is a counsellor who is neither shocked nor minimising: who takes the sin seriously without treating the person as beyond hope.

Heath Lambert’s Finally Free is an essential guide. His approach is thoroughly gospel-centred. The person caught in pornography needs not a more rigorous behaviour plan, but a deeper, more experiential encounter with the grace of Christ: grace greater than their shame, and powerful enough to produce the freedom willpower could not.

See a doctor, and begin now

Pornography addiction can overlap with depression, anxiety and other compulsive patterns that have physical components. Refer for a medical check-up, and begin counselling at the same time.

Understand the pattern

Before prescribing, ask: When does it usually happen — what time, what emotional state, what triggers? What are you feeling just before: loneliness, stress, boredom, rejection, anger? What does it give you in that moment: escape, power, comfort, a counterfeit intimacy? Is there a cycle of shame, isolation, pornography and more shame? Who knows about this? What would it mean for people to know?

The specific pattern of someone’s pornography use will reveal the specific idols of their heart. Do not apply generic counsel until you understand this person’s struggle.

Bought with a price

“Flee from sexual immorality… Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:18–20). Paul’s argument is theological, not merely moral. Sexual sin desecrates sacred space. But the same verses carry the gospel: this body has been purchased by Christ’s blood. It belongs to him. Brought not as condemnation but as identity, that truth gives a person something willpower cannot: a new reason to be free.

No condemnation

“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). This is the gospel antidote to the shame cycle that sustains pornography addiction. The person usually knows they are sinning, but the knowledge has not produced change, because it is buried under shame that drives them further into secrecy.

“No condemnation” does not minimise the sin. It relocates the person. They are in Christ. Their identity is not “addict” but child of God, bought with blood and indwelt by the Spirit. That identity, received by faith, repeated in prayer and confirmed in community, is the foundation of real freedom. No one escapes shame by trying harder. They escape it by believing more deeply in what Christ has done.

Into the light

Shame-driven secrecy is the environment in which this addiction thrives. Confession — real, specific, to a real person — is one of the most powerful interventions. “Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16). Helping someone move from secrecy to confession changes the environment their heart lives in. The patterns that darkness sustains cannot survive in the light.

Radical measures

Jesus said, “If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away” (Matthew 5:29). He commands ruthless removal of whatever gives access to sin. Filters and accountability software are not optional. Phones do not belong in the bedroom at vulnerable times. Late-night isolation must be broken. A person who says, “I want to be free, but I won’t change my circumstances,” does not yet understand what they are dealing with. Press this with firmness and grace.

When Potiphar’s wife grabbed Joseph, “he left his garment in her hand and fled and got out of the house” (Genesis 39:12). He did not negotiate or linger. He ran. That is the reflex to build: when temptation comes, respond physically and immediately. That is not weakness, but wisdom.

A practical plan

Alongside gospel counsel, four practical steps matter. Remove access. Break the secrecy with at least one trustworthy person who asks hard questions every week. Address the loneliness or stress that triggers the behaviour. And fill vulnerable moments with Scripture, prayer and contact with others. A useful exercise is to name the three most common triggers, and write a specific plan for each: what you will do instead, whom you will contact, and what Scripture you will pray.

The goal: glorifying God in the body

The goal is not merely freedom from pornography, but a life that glorifies God in the body. That means cultivating the opposite of the sin: real intimacy with God, with a spouse if married, and with accountable friends, and a life led by the Spirit. “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16).

The church’s part

A church that names pornography from the pulpit, makes room for honest confession and offers trained counselling is a church where people have a real chance of freedom. A church that never names it, or names it only with disgust, drives the struggle underground, where it grows in the dark until it destroys a marriage, a ministry or a soul. The Fighting Sin and Biblical Sexuality studies address this further.

For reflection

If someone confessed this struggle to you, would they meet disgust, minimising, or grace and truth together? What would help your church become a place where this can be brought into the light?

12.title: Hard Cases: Eating Disorders — Anorexia and Bulimia
12.essay:
Anorexia and bulimia are among the most medically dangerous conditions a pastor will meet. They are not phases, diets gone wrong or vanity. They are life-threatening patterns of thought and behaviour that must be taken with the utmost seriousness.

The danger

Anorexia carries one of the highest death rates of any psychiatric condition. Bulimia, the cycle of bingeing and purging, does serious damage over time: to the body’s chemistry, the digestive system, the teeth and the heart.

See a doctor immediately, and begin counselling now

Do not wait for the medical appointment before you begin to counsel; both happen at once. The body needs urgent medical attention, and the soul needs the word of God at the same time. A team approach — a doctor, perhaps a dietitian, and biblical counselling — is not compromise. It is wise stewardship of body and soul, which God made as one. If a person’s weight or health is at a life-threatening level, emergency medical care comes first.

The heart beneath the behaviour

Anorexia restricts; bulimia binges and purges. But the heart issues often overlap: a desperate need for control in a life that feels chaotic, an identity built on body image, deep shame about the self, and a perfectionism that punishes every failure. Amy Baker’s Picture Perfect addresses the roots of perfectionism and shame with particular insight. Both conditions can also become ways of managing overwhelming emotions: eating, or not eating, works as regulation, escape or punishment.

Take time to understand

Take significant time before prescribing anything. When did this begin? Was there a trigger: a loss, or a time when your sense of control was taken away? What does restricting, or bingeing and purging, give you? What do you believe about your body, your worth, and what you must be to be acceptable — to yourself, to others, to God? What are you most afraid would happen if you gained weight, or if people knew? Who knows about this? What does perfectionism look like in other areas of your life? The answers will show whether the heart struggle is mainly about control, shame, perfectionism, emotional regulation, or a mixture.

Fearfully and wonderfully made

“For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother’s womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalm 139:13–14). This is the counter-narrative to the disorder’s core lie: my body is wrong, shameful, too much, not enough. God formed this body, this specific body, not a thinner or more perfect version, with intention and care.

But the counsellor must not use this verse quickly or superficially. It is a truth to return to again and again, to pray over and soak in, because the disorder’s lies have been repeated far longer and more insistently.

The gospel speaks

To the person whose identity rests on control and perfection, the gospel says: in Christ you are already perfectly accepted, not because of what you weigh or how much control you keep, but because of what he has done. You are not your performance. You are his.

To the person caught in a cycle of shame and secrecy, it says: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Purging does not purify; only the blood of Christ does. The shame that drives the secrecy is met by a Saviour who already knows everything and has already paid for everything. That is not a quick fix. But received deeply and returned to often, it begins to loosen the disorder’s grip.

Law without gospel

Perfectionism is, at root, a theological problem: law without gospel, performance without grace, self-justification through self-punishment. The gospel’s answer is not lower standards, but a different foundation: worth that is given, not earned, resting on the finished work of Christ rather than numbers on a scale.

The body matters to God

The incarnation, God taking flesh, and the resurrection, Jesus rising in a body, show that the body is not incidental to who we are. So caring for the body in recovery is not a distraction from spiritual work. It is part of it.

“Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit… So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). That is not said to condemn, but to restore the dignity and purpose that the disorder has stolen. The goal is not a number on a scale. It is a person who increasingly receives their body as a gift from God, a dwelling of the Spirit, to be cared for rather than punished, controlled or hidden.

Received, not despised

A woman known in her town as “a sinner” came to Jesus at a dinner and wept over his feet, wiping them with her hair and anointing them with ointment. The host was disgusted. Jesus received her, defended her, and said, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7:50). Someone with an eating disorder has often experienced their body as a source of shame. The Jesus who received that woman without disgust, and with honour, is the Jesus who can rebuild a person’s relationship with their own body.

A long road

Prepare for a long engagement, measured in years rather than weeks. It needs patience, consistency and trust built slowly. The counsellor who keeps showing up, and does not give up after setbacks, embodies the persistence of grace. Do not go it alone: involve the medical team, the family (carefully), and the church as a network of support.

Every meal eaten in gratitude, every choice of nourishment over restriction or purging, every day of telling the truth to a trusted person, is an act of worship. With the medical team’s guidance, a person might set one specific eating goal for the week, and write down one lie the disorder tells them about their body, alongside one true thing God says.

For reflection

Is there someone in your church who may be struggling in this way, perhaps in secret? How could you help them find both medical help and gospel care?

13.title: Hard Cases: Alcohol and Drug Addiction
13.essay:
Alcohol and drug addiction combine physical dependency with deep heart issues. That is exactly why both must be addressed, and neither ignored.

Both at once

A pastor who addresses only the spiritual dimension while ignoring the physical is naive. A medical professional who treats only the body while ignoring the heart will see the person return again and again. Begin both at the same time.

A medical emergency

Alcohol withdrawal in someone who is physically dependent can be fatal, causing seizures and death. Never tell a dependent person simply to stop drinking without medical supervision. If withdrawal is a risk, get them to a doctor or hospital immediately. Drug withdrawal also needs medical assessment. Counselling begins alongside medical care, not after it.

A banquet in the grave

Edward Welch’s Addictions: A Banquet in the Grave is an essential guide. Its title comes from Proverbs, which describes the guests at the table of Folly: “But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol” (Proverbs 9:18). Welch argues that addiction is at heart about worship. The substance has become the go-to comfort, escape and pleasure, a functional god that promises what only the true God can give, and takes everything in payment.

This does not deny the physical reality of dependency; sustained substance use genuinely alters the brain. But it names the spiritual root beneath the physical symptom. Treat the body with medicine and the heart with the gospel, together.

Questions to ask

Ask carefully and without judgment. When did heavy use begin — was there a particular period, pain or loss? What does it give you that you do not feel otherwise? What are you trying to escape, or numb? What is the hardest thing about being sober? What have you already lost — family, work, health, self-respect? Have you tried to stop before, and what happened? Honestly, do you believe God could free you? You need to understand what void the substance is filling, in order to point to the One who can truly fill it.

Slavery and freedom

Jesus named the condition precisely: “Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin” (John 8:34). The person who has tried to stop and cannot is not merely weak-willed. They are experiencing the bondage sin always produces when indulged over time. But the diagnosis serves the promise: “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36). That is what an addicted person most needs to hear: not “try harder,” but “there is a Liberator.”

We ourselves were once

Paul writes, “For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures” (Titus 3:3). That is the counsellor’s own story before it is the counselee’s diagnosis. A counsellor who can say it honestly offers identification, not superiority. Then Paul goes on: “But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy” (Titus 3:4–5). The gospel changes addicts the way it changes everyone: not by willpower, but by the Spirit’s renewal of the heart, giving it a new desire — for God, rather than the substance.

Not alone

“Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm” (Proverbs 13:20). Recovery without community is rare. The person needs to be embedded in a community that knows their struggle, checks in regularly, provides alternatives to the isolation that sustains addiction, and shows the grace of Christ in response to failure. Recovery groups can help, but the church is God’s primary family for this.

The running father

The prodigal son squandered everything in reckless living and ended up feeding pigs. His turning point was a memory: “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!” (Luke 15:17). And when he came home, “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). The counsellor represents that running father, coming towards the person in the pigsty before they have cleaned themselves up.

Planning for relapse

Relapse is very common in recovery and should be planned for, not treated as a catastrophe. Say in advance: “If you fall, call me. Don’t disappear into shame.” That removes one of the most dangerous dynamics: the shame that drives someone underground after a failure and makes the next fall more likely. Grace must be more accessible than shame.

Practical steps

Alongside gospel counsel: medical supervision for withdrawal; removing access as completely as possible; a community of accountability that knows and checks in; addressing the pain, loneliness or stress the substance was numbing; and filling the time and space the substance occupied with prayer, Scripture, fellowship and service, not just absence. It helps to name the three situations or feelings most likely to trigger use, and write a specific plan for each: whom to call, what to pray, and where to go instead.

The goal: true satisfaction

Sobriety is necessary, but it is not the final goal. The goal is a person who no longer needs the substance because they are finding in Christ what it promised but never delivered: real comfort, peace, belonging and lasting joy. It is the transformation of worship, from the idol to the living God.

For reflection

Where do you turn first for comfort or escape? How could your church become a place where people fighting addiction find both accountability and grace?

14.title: Hard Cases: Gambling Addiction
14.essay:
Gambling addiction is often overlooked in pastoral care, yet it is among the most financially and relationally destructive patterns a pastor will meet.

Hidden damage

The person in its grip has often lost not only money, but family savings, a home, a marriage and their self-respect, and still cannot stop. The shame is enormous and the secrecy almost universal. The damage usually stays hidden until a crisis forces it into the open.

The idols beneath

The heart issues are specific and worth naming. There is often an idol of fortune and control: the belief that I can beat the odds, that I have a system, that the next bet will be different. There may be a deep anxiety about provision, which gambling paradoxically tries to solve. Sometimes there is pride that cannot accept ordinary financial limits, or a craving for the excitement ordinary life does not give. Brad Bigney’s approach to diagnosing idols applies directly.

See a doctor, and begin now

Compulsive gambling is often linked with depression, anxiety and problems of impulse control. Refer for a medical check-up, and begin counselling at the same time. And if financial desperation brings any risk of self-harm, treat it as a suicide risk and follow the guidance in the chapter on suicide and self-harm.

Questions to ask

When did this begin — was there an early win that hooked you? What does gambling give you that ordinary life does not: excitement, hope, a feeling of being lucky or special? What are you most anxious about, financially or otherwise, and is gambling an attempt to fix it? Do you believe you can win back what you have lost? How much have you lost in total, honestly? Who knows? What do you think will happen if nothing changes?

The belief that the next bet will be different is a form of magical thinking: a functional trust in luck rather than God. Naming that gently opens the door to the gospel’s real offer, a provision and a future that do not depend on chance.

Great gain

“But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world” (1 Timothy 6:6–7). Paul’s definition of gain is the opposite of the gambler’s pursuit. We are all playing with borrowed chips, on borrowed time, in a world we did not create and cannot control. Paul offers not poverty but contentment: a settled sufficiency that does not need the jackpot, because it has already received the inheritance. What a gambler seeks at the bookmaker’s — security, significance, a safe future — is already theirs in Christ, freely and without risk.

The lie of the shortcut

Proverbs warns repeatedly against seeking wealth by shortcuts. “Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it” (Proverbs 13:11). “A stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty will come upon him” (Proverbs 28:22). Lasting provision comes through faithful work, honest dealing and patient saving, not chance. And the love of money is “a root of all kinds of evils” (1 Timothy 6:10).

Your Father knows

Gambling often numbs a deeper anxiety: will there be enough? Will I be all right? Jesus’ answer is not that the numbers will work out, but that “your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:32). And Paul promises, “my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19). The counsellor helps the person move from trusting luck to trusting the Father.

Learning contentment

“I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content” (Philippians 4:11). And “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13), including living within ordinary means, without the thrill of the bet or the fantasy of the win. Contentment is learned, not instantly given. It grows through trust practised in specific situations, one ordinary day and one unglamorous provision at a time.

Practical steps

Total transparency about money with a spouse or an accountability partner. Removing all access — no betting shops, apps or online accounts — by structural barriers, not just good intentions. Facing the debts honestly, with a trusted debt adviser if needed; many Christian charities offer free debt counselling. Addressing the anxiety or boredom gambling was numbing. And developing a theology of work and provision: God provides through faithful work and wise stewardship, not chance. One helpful exercise is to record every financial decision for a week, with one thing you thanked God for in each.

The family

The damage to families is often enormous. Spouses and children who have been lied to, whose savings have gone and whose trust has been broken again and again, need pastoral care of their own. A counsellor who cares for the whole family, not just the gambler, is addressing the full scope of what the addiction has done.

The goal: faithful stewardship

The goal is not merely debt management or abstinence. It is a person who increasingly glorifies God through faithful stewardship of what they have been given, and who has found in him the security they were chasing.

For reflection

Where do you look for security about the future? What would it mean to trust that your heavenly Father knows what you need?

15.title: Hard Cases: Severe Mental Illness
15.essay:
Severe mental illness — schizophrenia, psychosis, severe bipolar disorder with psychotic features — is among the hardest situations a pastor will face, and among the most important to handle with humility.

A psychiatrist first

A person who is hearing voices, holding fixed false beliefs, or has lost touch with reality is not, in that acute moment, primarily in need of counselling. They need a psychiatrist. The pastor’s role here is not primary treatment, but faithful, long-term presence alongside medical care.

That is not a retreat from the sufficiency of Scripture. It is an application of it. Scripture teaches that we are embodied creatures, that the fall has affected all of creation, including the brain, and that the body may need medicine as the soul needs the word. These truths are complementary, not competing.

Get help, and stay present

Acute psychosis needs emergency psychiatric assessment. Do not wait. But do not withdraw either. Begin pastoral presence — visiting, praying, keeping in touch — alongside medical care. The church’s presence does not depend on the medical situation being resolved.

Questions to ask

In severe mental illness, questions are often directed to the family as much as to the person, who may not be reachable during an acute episode. How long has this been happening? Is there a diagnosis? Is the person under psychiatric care, and taking medication consistently? Is there a crisis plan? What does their best functioning look like — what can they do, what do they enjoy, what connects them to God and others? What does the family need right now?

With the person themselves, in a stable period: How do you feel about your diagnosis? What do you find most helpful? What do you believe God thinks of you in this? What gives you hope?

Creation groaning
