“For the creation was subjected to futility… For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now” (Romans 8:20–22). The fall corrupted the whole creation, the brain included. Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and psychosis are not spiritual failures or divine punishments. They are part of creation’s groaning under the fall.

The person with severe mental illness is suffering under a brokenness they did not choose and cannot simply repent their way out of. A wise counsellor will not demand spiritual performance from someone whose brain is not working normally, nor read symptoms as evidence of weak faith.

A bruised reed

Isaiah describes the Servant’s gentleness: “a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench” (Isaiah 42:3). That is Jesus’ pastoral policy towards the fragile. The person with severe mental illness is often the bruised reed, barely standing, and the faint wick, more smoke than flame. Jesus does not break or snuff them out. He tends them patiently. A pastor who visits the psychiatric ward, keeps up the relationship through hospital stays, and treats the person with dignity, is embodying the character of the One who tends bruised reeds.

Blame it on the brain?

Edward Welch’s Blame It on the Brain? gives a helpful framework. The brain is an organ, and like any organ it can malfunction because of the fall. A malfunctioning brain affects thought, emotion and perception. But it does not change the person’s standing before God, their identity in Christ, or God’s love for them. The counsellor holds both truths: this person needs medical help for their brain, and pastoral care for their soul. Neither cancels the other.

The family

Caring for a family member with severe mental illness is one of the most exhausting and isolating experiences anyone can face. The church’s care for the family — practical help, respite, prayer, honest acknowledgment of how hard it is — is as important as its care for the person who is ill.

Nebuchadnezzar

Nebuchadnezzar’s madness is the Bible’s most dramatic picture of what looks like severe mental breakdown: he lived like an animal, cut off from human society. Yet God was sovereign over it, and at the end he said, “my reason returned to me, and I blessed the Most High” (Daniel 4:34). Not every severe illness resolves this way. But God is not absent from even the worst episodes, and his purposes are not defeated by them.

Plan before the crisis

Every congregation should have a plan before a psychiatric crisis comes. Whom do we call? Who will go with the person to hospital? Who will support the family? Who will keep up pastoral contact during a hospital stay? A church that has thought these through beforehand will respond far more faithfully than one that scrambles in the moment.

The goal: faithful presence

The goal here is not cure, though we pray for it. It is faithful presence: surrounding the person and their family with consistent, non-abandoning love. Even in the most severe cases, the church can do what no medication can: affirm the person’s identity in Christ when their own mind cannot reliably do so, keep them connected and belonging, support an exhausted family, and hold on to hope when they cannot. A simple step this week: one visit, one meal, one phone call.

For reflection

Does your church have a plan for supporting someone in a mental health crisis, and their family? How could you be a faithful presence to someone who is fragile?

16.title: Hard Cases: OCD and Intrusive Thoughts
16.essay:
Few people in a congregation suffer more quietly and alone than those tormented by intrusive thoughts. They need a counsellor who understands what is happening, and what is not.

What intrusive thoughts are

Intrusive thoughts are unwanted, involuntary thoughts that horrify the person who has them: thoughts of harming someone they love, blasphemous thoughts about God, sexual thoughts about inappropriate people, or violent images that arrive uninvited. Crucially, the person is not planning to act on them. They are desperately trying to make them stop. And the harder they try, the louder the thoughts become, because obsessive-compulsive disorder feeds on resistance.

Scrupulosity

In scrupulosity, the religious form of OCD, the person cannot shake the conviction that they have committed an unforgivable sin, that their intrusive thoughts mean they have blasphemed the Holy Spirit, or that God has rejected them. This is pastorally treacherous ground. A counsellor who answers each fear with simple reassurance (“you’re fine”) triggers the next cycle. But one who takes every fear at face value and offers long theological explanations also feeds the compulsive need for reassurance that keeps the disorder going.

See a doctor, and begin now

OCD has neurological components and responds to specific treatment, especially a therapy called exposure and response prevention, alongside pastoral care. Refer for a psychiatric assessment straight away, and begin counselling at the same time. The two work together.

Understand the cycle

Ask carefully: Can you describe a typical intrusive thought, and when it tends to come? How do you respond — do you try to suppress it, argue with it, seek reassurance, or do some ritual to neutralise it? How long has this been happening? Do the thoughts cluster around particular fears: harm, blasphemy, contamination, sexual sin? Does reassurance help, or only briefly? Do you believe the thoughts reveal who you really are?

Understand the cycle before intervening: obsession, then anxiety, then compulsion, then temporary relief, then the obsession returns. And understand this above all: these thoughts are not the person’s desires. They are the opposite of desire.

The thought is not the sin

James describes how sin works: “But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death” (James 1:14–15). Sin begins with desire, the heart’s willing movement towards what it wants.

Intrusive thoughts are not that. The person tormented by violent or blasphemous thoughts does not want them. They are horrified by them. James is describing the willing entertaining of desire, not an unwanted intrusion. A counsellor who helps the person grasp this distinction, clearly and repeatedly, lifts one of their heaviest burdens: the false belief that having a thought means wanting it, and wanting it means being it. The thought is not the sin.

Confusing the two does enormous damage. Temptation is something the flesh welcomes. An intrusive thought is something the person hates. A counsellor who treats OCD thoughts as evidence of spiritual failure has misdiagnosed the situation and will add suffering to suffering.

No condemnation

“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). For the scrupulous person, this must be applied precisely and patiently. No condemnation: not reduced, not conditional, not suspended pending performance. None. Do not add conditions Paul does not add.

The OCD will always find another sin to worry about and another reassurance to seek. So the pastoral response is not an exhaustive theological reassurance, which feeds the cycle, but a gentle, firm return to the anchor: you are in Christ. That is settled. Return to Christ, not to the fear. Jesus has promised, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

Redirect, don’t reassure

Providing extensive reassurance feels like pastoral care, but it actually feeds the cycle: the relief reinforces the seeking, which intensifies the next episode. The wiser response, learned from good treatment, is to give brief, general reassurance while declining to engage the specific fear in detail. That feels less pastoral at first, as if you are refusing to answer. But a person who discovers that Christ is sufficient even while a fear remains unresolved is helped far more than one who receives another round of reassurance that lasts only until the next intrusive thought.

Taking thoughts captive

Paul speaks of taking “every thought captive to obey Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). In the context of OCD, that does not mean fighting or suppressing the thought, which intensifies it. It means noticing it, naming it — “that is an intrusive thought, not a desire and not a sin” — and turning attention to Christ, rather than to arguing with the thought or seeking reassurance.

In practice: do not seek reassurance when an intrusive thought strikes, whether from a counsellor, from Scripture used compulsively, or from others. Practise tolerating the anxiety without the compulsion. And return to a settled trust in Christ, rather than a reactive struggle with the thought. When the next one comes, it can help to write it down, write beside it “this is a thought, not a desire, not a sin,” and add one truth about who you are in Christ.

Luther’s prison

Martin Luther’s scrupulosity is well known: his fear of never having confessed enough, his terror that he had sinned beyond God’s reach. His mentor Johann von Staupitz reportedly told him to come back with a real sin worth forgiving instead of trifles. It was not dismissal, but a pastoral instinct to break the cycle of endless self-examination and point Luther to the cross. The Reformation’s great discovery, justification by faith alone, was in part Luther’s escape from that prison. The person with OCD today is often living in Luther’s darkness before the light dawned. The gospel is the way out.

The goal: held loosely

The goal is a person who can hold an intrusive thought loosely, acknowledging it without being controlled by it, and whose identity rests on their standing in Christ, not on the absence of difficult thoughts.

For reflection

Why is it so important to distinguish intrusive thoughts from sinful desires? How could you offer someone the anchor of Christ without feeding the cycle of reassurance?

17.title: Hard Cases: Trauma and Sexual Abuse
17.essay:
Trauma, and sexual abuse in particular, asks of a counsellor a posture before it asks a technique: slowness, gentleness, complete trustworthiness, and a willingness to listen without fixing.

The first five minutes

A person who has been sexually abused has had their body violated, their trust shattered, often by someone they knew and trusted, and their sense that the world is safe destroyed. They may have carried this in silence for years or decades.

The pastor who receives that disclosure holds a moment of enormous importance. Their response in the next few minutes will either confirm that it is finally safe to speak, or confirm the person’s deepest fear that no one can be trusted with this. Go slowly. Listen far more than you speak. Do not minimise, spiritualise too soon, or rush towards forgiveness before the person has been truly heard.

Abused people often carry false guilt; they have been told, or have concluded, that it was somehow their fault. So the counsellor’s first and most essential task is to say, clearly and compassionately: what was done to you was wrong. It was not your fault. You are not alone.

Safety and reporting

Trauma affects the body; severe and repeated trauma, especially in childhood, genuinely affects the brain. Refer for a medical assessment, particularly if there are physical symptoms, sleep problems or dissociation, and begin counselling alongside it.

And know your legal and safeguarding duties. If a child is currently at risk, or abuse is ongoing, report it to the authorities immediately, and involve your church’s safeguarding lead. That is not a betrayal of confidence. It is the protection of the vulnerable that Scripture commands: “Give justice to the weak and the fatherless… Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked” (Psalm 82:3–4).

Questions, slowly

Before asking anything, establish safety: “I’m grateful you’ve trusted me with this. There’s no pressure to share more than you’re ready to. I’m going to listen.” Then, slowly, and only as trust grows: How old were you? Was it once, or repeated? Who did this? Are you safe now? Have you ever told anyone before? What has made it hardest to speak about? What do you believe about yourself because of what happened? What do you believe about God — near or distant, trustworthy or absent? Take weeks, not one conversation, to understand the whole picture. Safety must come before the application of truth.

God has not hidden his face

“For he has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, and he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard, when he cried to him” (Psalm 22:24). God does not turn away from what was done to an abused person in disgust or embarrassment. He hears. The counsellor communicates this not by quoting the verse quickly, but by their own attentive presence that does not turn away.

A High Priest who has been there

The Son of God knows violation and suffering from the inside. He was betrayed by a trusted companion. He was stripped. He was publicly shamed. He cried out in abandonment. “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15). And so, “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). A survivor can come to God with their wounds rather than hiding them.

Shame is a lie

Sexual abuse almost always produces shame: not godly sorrow that leads to repentance, but the toxic shame that says, “I am damaged, defiled, permanently broken.” That shame is a lie, and the counsellor speaks truth against it, patiently and persistently. The person is still made in God’s image, loved by Christ, purchased by his blood, and, if they are a believer, indwelt by the Spirit. What was done to the body does not undo what God has done for the soul.

Tamar

Tamar’s story is the Bible’s most painful account of sexual abuse within a family. She pleaded, “No, my brother, do not violate me” (2 Samuel 13:12). Afterwards, “Tamar lived, a desolate woman, in her brother Absalom’s house” (2 Samuel 13:20). And notice what did not happen. “When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry” (2 Samuel 13:21), but he did nothing. No one stood with Tamar, spoke for her, or pursued justice, and the silence bred more tragedy. A church that does what the palace failed to do — stands with the abused, speaks for the vulnerable, and pursues justice — is being the community God designed it to be.

Beauty for ashes

The goal is not the absence of pain. It is a person who can bring their full history into God’s presence, find that he receives it without flinching, and gradually be rebuilt as someone defined not by what was done to them, but by who they are in Christ. God promises “a beautiful headdress instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the garment of praise instead of a faint spirit” (Isaiah 61:3). That is not a quick exchange, but a slow work of the Spirit. “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds” (Psalm 147:3).

Forgiveness, in time

Forgiving the abuser, where it becomes possible, is a long-term hope, never rushed or demanded. It is God’s gift at the right time, not a precondition of healing. And it never means trusting the abuser again, keeping silent, or shielding them from justice.

Caring for the carer

Those who work with trauma must look after their own souls. Absorbing others’ worst stories takes a real toll. Regular supervision or consultation, steady rhythms of prayer and rest, and honest friendships with people who know what you carry are essential. Sustaining yourself is not selfishness. It is what makes sustained faithfulness possible.

For reflection

If someone disclosed abuse to you, what would you say in the first few minutes? Does your church know its safeguarding duties, and how to stand with survivors?

18.title: Hard Cases: Suicide and Self-Harm
18.essay:
Suicide is the pastoral emergency above all others. A person who is actively suicidal is in immediate danger of death, and the pastor’s response may be the difference between life and death. Prepare before the crisis comes.

If there is immediate risk

If someone tells you they intend to end their life and have a plan and the means, act at once. Do not leave them alone. Call the emergency services (999 in the UK, 112 across Europe, 911 in North America) or take them to an emergency department. Do not promise to keep active suicidal intent confidential. Remove access to the means if you can, and ask directly about medication stockpiles, weapons and other methods. Contact family or a trusted person to stay with them. Follow up every day until the crisis has passed and professional support is in place. This is not a matter for an appointment next week. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be reached at any hour on 116 123.

Ask directly

Asking about suicide does not increase the risk, and it may reduce it by opening the door. So ask plainly: Are you thinking about ending your life? Do you have a plan? Do you have the means? Have you tried before? Is anything keeping you from acting right now?

Once immediate risk has been assessed, seek to understand the pain. What has brought you here? What feels unbearable? What do you think would happen to the people you love? Where is God in this for you right now? Is there any part of you that wants to be here, that wants things to be different? That part, the part that wants to live, is the part to reach.

Elijah again

Elijah, the prophet of fire, sat under a broom tree and “asked that he might die, saying, ‘It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life’” (1 Kings 19:4). God did not rebuke him. He did not call his despair unbelief and command repentance. He let him sleep, and sent an angel to touch him and say, “Arise and eat” (1 Kings 19:5). Before any theology, before any new commission, food and rest. The counsellor does the same: attend to immediate needs — safety, sleep, food — before pressing into spiritual questions, and meet the person where they are.

Nothing can separate

“For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39). That is the gospel’s answer to the suicidal person’s deepest fear: that they are beyond reach. Not the death they are considering, not the life that feels unbearable, not the depth of their despair. God’s love in Christ does not depend on stability, performance or strength of faith. It is the love of One who has already gone into the darkest place — the cross, the tomb — and come out the other side.

A prayer for the darkest place

Psalm 88 ends in darkness: “my companions have become darkness” (Psalm 88:18). It is in the Bible. So even absolute despair, the life that sees no light, is within the scope of prayer. A person in suicidal darkness who prays Psalm 88 is doing something remarkable: bringing their despair to God rather than away from him. A counsellor who can sit with that prayer, without needing to resolve it, offers something more valuable than any technique.

Life belongs to God

The church has historically regarded suicide as a grave sin, the taking of a life that belongs to God. That conviction must be held with pastoral wisdom. A person in crisis does not first need a lecture on the sinfulness of suicide. They need care, presence and hope. The truth that their life belongs to God is better conveyed by a community that stays close and refuses to abandon them than by a statement delivered in the middle of the crisis. And for families bereaved by suicide, the church must offer comfort, not condemnation, entrusting their loved one to a merciful God.

Self-harm

Self-harm without suicidal intent — cutting, burning, hitting — is different, but also serious. It is usually a way of managing overwhelming emotional pain: physical pain gives a brief release from unbearable inner pain. It needs medical care for the wounds and the risk of infection, and ongoing counselling. Begin both immediately. The counsellor asks what is so overwhelming that this feels like the only relief, and points gently to a different relief: “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding” (Philippians 4:7), which does not require self-harm to reach.

The goal: staying alive

In the acute phase, the goal is one thing: staying alive. Everything else is secondary. Once safety is established, a longer goal emerges: helping the person discover that life, even painful life, can be lived to the glory of God; that their story is not finished, there are people yet to love, and God has not finished with them. Someone who survives a suicidal crisis and comes to trust God through the darkness often becomes one of the most powerful witnesses to his faithfulness a church has. In the recovery phase, a small but meaningful step is to write down one reason to be alive each week, however small.

A plan before the crisis

Every congregation should prepare a response plan before a crisis occurs. Who is trained to assess risk? Who can be reached at any hour? What is the link with local emergency and mental health services? Who provides follow-up after a hospital stay? A church that has thought these through is far better equipped to stay close when the darkness comes.

For reflection

Would you know what to do if someone told you they wanted to end their life? Take a moment now to note your local emergency number and a crisis line, and pray for anyone you know who is in darkness.

19.title: Hard Cases: Domestic Violence and Abuse
19.essay:
Domestic abuse is one of the most dangerous and most frequently mishandled situations in the church. The first and non-negotiable priority is the safety of the abused person and any children.

Why it is mishandled

It is dangerous because abusers are often charming, active in church, and skilled at presenting themselves as the victim. It is mishandled because pastors trained in the theology of reconciliation often apply marriage-preservation principles to a situation that needs safety-first principles, and send an abused spouse back into danger with advice to pray more or be more submissive.

Safety first

Before counselling, before marriage restoration, before theological discussion, the first question is: is this person safe? If not, secure their safety. That may mean helping them reach a refuge, explaining their legal options, and, if children are at risk, making a safeguarding report to the authorities. In the UK, the National Domestic Abuse Helpline is available day and night. In an emergency, call the police.

Domestic abuse is not a conflict problem needing conflict resolution. It is a problem of power and control needing accountability and protection. So do not bring the abuser and the abused together for joint counselling until the abuser has shown sustained, verified repentance over a significant period. Premature couples counselling gives an abuser new information to weaponise and new leverage to use.

Questions to ask

Ask privately, never with the suspected abuser present. Are you safe at home? Has your partner ever hit you, choked you, or threatened to hurt you or the children? Do they control your money, your friendships, your movements? Have they threatened to harm themselves or others if you leave? Do you feel free to come and go, to see friends and family, to disagree? Are the children safe? Have you ever felt afraid of them?

Abused people often minimise, explain away, or protect the abuser. Specific, gentle questions asked without judgment create the safety in which the truth can emerge. Recognised frameworks that map patterns of power and control can be useful practical tools here.

Justice first

“He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). Justice is named first. In domestic abuse, justice means naming what is happening accurately — abuse, not “conflict” — protecting the vulnerable, holding the powerful to account, and not restoring a relationship that is not yet safe. A pastor who puts the preservation of a marriage above the safety of an abused spouse has misapplied the theology of marriage. God designed marriage for the flourishing of both, not as a trap.

Submission is not a cage

The teaching on wives’ submission (Ephesians 5:22–24) has been badly misused here. It must be read with what follows: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). A husband who terrorises his wife has not misunderstood submission; he has abandoned his own calling. No biblical teaching on submission requires anyone to remain in ongoing physical danger. And the same is true whichever spouse is the abuser.

The gospel for both

To the abused person, the gospel says: what is being done to you is wrong. God sees it. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit” (Psalm 34:18). This was never his intention for you. You are not trapped by a theology that requires you to stay in danger. Your safety, and your children’s safety, matter to God.

To the abuser, separately and with proper accountability, it says: what you are doing is serious sin, against a person made in God’s image, against your vows, against your children and against God. The gospel offers real forgiveness and the Spirit’s power to change. But change must be real, sustained and verified before any restoration can be considered. Words of repentance are not enough. Changed patterns of behaviour over time are the evidence.

Protection, accountability, possible restoration

The goal is not divorce, nor the preservation of the marriage at any cost. Where abuse persists and the abuser will not repent, Reformed churches have rightly treated it as a form of desertion that frees the victim: “In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved” (1 Corinthians 7:15). The goal is justice: protection for the vulnerable, accountability for the abuser, and — only if genuine repentance is shown over a verified period — the possible rebuilding of a relationship on a wholly different foundation.

In practice: secure immediate safety. Counsel each person separately, never together in the acute phase. Put the abuser under a structured process of accountability, with specific behavioural requirements, involving the elders and, where there is a crime, the law. Give the abused person pastoral care, practical support, and help rebuilding an identity in Christ that the abuse has damaged. And where the abuser is unrepentant, exercise church discipline (Matthew 18:15–17). A pastor who does so is not destroying a marriage, but seeking to save a soul. Protection of the vulnerable never waits on that hope. A simple first step for an abused person is to identify one safe person they can call if things escalate, keep the number in more than one place, and tell them what is happening.

Abigail

Abigail was married to Nabal, a man described as “harsh and badly behaved” (1 Samuel 25:3). When his folly put the whole household in danger, she took decisive, independent action to protect them and to prevent violence, and Scripture presents her wisdom as entirely right. A woman who acts to protect herself and her children is following a good biblical precedent.

A safe church

The church must become a place where abused people feel safe enough to tell the truth. That means preaching that names abuse plainly as sin, trained people who know how to receive a disclosure, clear safeguarding procedures, and a culture that never shames victims or protects powerful abusers. A congregation that has done this work before a crisis will respond faithfully when one comes.

For reflection

Would someone suffering abuse in your church feel safe enough to tell you? What would you do first if they did?

20.title: Hard Cases: Alzheimer’s and Other Dementias
20.essay:
Dementia slowly takes memory, words, judgment and sometimes personality. It does not take a person out of God’s hand. This chapter is about how to love someone with dementia, how to speak with them, and how to keep their carers from going under.

What dementia is

Dementia is not normal ageing. It is a disease of the brain that gets worse over time. Alzheimer’s is the most common form. Vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia and frontotemporal dementia are others, and each looks a little different. Short-term memory usually goes first. Long-term memory, music, prayer and habits learnt in childhood often last much longer.

So the medical principle applies with full force. Ask for a proper diagnosis. Some things that look like dementia can be treated, such as depression, thyroid problems, a lack of vitamin B12, or side effects of medication. A sudden change in confusion often has a physical cause, such as an infection, and needs a doctor the same day.

Still a person, still God’s

Our culture tends to measure a person by what they can remember, decide and do. Scripture measures a person by the God who made them. The image of God is not stored in the memory, and it does not fade as the memory fades. The woman who no longer knows her children is still someone God knit together in her mother’s womb (Psalm 139:13).

And God makes this promise to the old: “even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save” (Isaiah 46:4). He is the one who carries. The believer with dementia is not held by her grip on God, but by his grip on her. “No one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). “If we are faithless, he remains faithful—for he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13).

The deepest comfort is this. She may forget God, but God does not forget her. “Can a woman forget her nursing child…? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15). John Swinton puts it well: we are held in the memory of God.

What it does not mean

Forgetting God is not falling away from God. A Christian who can no longer pray, or who says confused or even bitter things about God, is not showing what is truly in their heart. They are showing what the disease has done to the brain. In the same way, outbursts, crude words or suspicion (“you stole my purse”) are usually symptoms, not sins to be confronted. Moral responsibility shrinks as the ability to understand shrinks. Do not counsel the later stages of dementia as if you were counselling sin. Comfort, protect and stay close.

In the early stages

Early on, the person can still be counselled, and they usually have real fears: of losing themselves, of being a burden, of being forgotten. Talk with them, not about them in front of them. Psalm 23 speaks straight to this fear: “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me” (Psalm 23:4).

This is also the time to plan while they still can. Help them set up legal authority for someone they trust to make decisions later (in the UK, a lasting power of attorney). Write down their wishes for care and for their funeral, their favourite hymns and psalms, and their testimony in their own words. Encourage them to say what needs saying to their family now. These are acts of love for the family who will carry them later.

How to talk with someone with dementia

A few simple habits make a great difference. Say who you are each time: “Hello, Margaret, it’s Tom from church.” Do not test them with “Do you remember me?” Sit at eye level, speak slowly and calmly, and use short sentences. Ask one simple question at a time, and give them time to answer. Questions with a yes or no answer, or a choice of two, are easier than open questions.

Do not argue or keep correcting. If she says she must go and collect the children from school, you will not win the argument, and she will only feel frightened. Respond to the feeling behind the words: “You love your children. Tell me about them.” Often the feeling is the real message.

Remember that behaviour is communication. Restlessness, shouting or striking out may mean pain, hunger, needing the toilet, being too hot, or fear. Look for the need before you look for a solution.

Truth and kindness

Christians disagree about one hard question. When a man asks every day where his wife is, and she died three years ago, should you tell him? Each time he hears it, he grieves as if for the first time. Some carers simply go along with whatever he believes, even if that means saying untrue things, because they think kindness requires it. Others insist on telling him the facts every time, because they think honesty requires it.

A better way respects both truth and love. Do not lie, because God is truth and the ninth commandment still applies. But you are not obliged to say every true thing at every moment. You can gently turn to what he is feeling and what he remembers: “You’re thinking about Joan. You loved her very much. Tell me how you met.” This is neither deceit nor cruelty. It is speaking the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), at a pace a failing mind can bear.

What still reaches them

The parts of the mind that hold music, rhythm and prayer often last the longest. So sing the hymns they learnt as children. Pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly and let them join in. Read Psalm 23 in the translation they memorised, even if it is not the one your church now uses. Hold their hand. Many pastors have watched a woman who could not say her daughter’s name sing every verse of a hymn and then say “Amen.” It is the word of God, stored long ago, still speaking.

Keep visiting

People with dementia are among the most forgotten people in the church. Visitors stop coming, often with the thought, “She won’t remember I was there anyway.” But the visit is not for her memory. It is for her, now, in the moment, and it is done for Christ himself: “I was sick and you visited me” (Matthew 25:36). Short, regular visits are better than long, rare ones. A twenty-minute visit on a Tuesday afternoon, with one psalm, one hymn and a hand to hold, is real ministry, even if it leaves no memory but in heaven.

The Lord’s Supper

Should a believer with advanced dementia still receive the Supper? Some say no, because Paul says, “Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup” (1 Corinthians 11:28), and she can no longer examine herself. Others say yes, because she is a member in good standing, her faith was professed and tested over many years, and the Supper is a sign of Christ holding her, not of her holding him.

The second view seems wiser. Paul’s command addresses people who are able to examine themselves and are failing to do so. It does not cut off a faithful member because of a disease. Elders should judge each case with care, but in general a long-professing member who can still receive it peacefully should not be excluded from her Lord’s table by an illness she did not choose.

Caring for the carers

The heaviest burden often falls on a husband, a wife or a daughter. Caring for someone with dementia is one of the most exhausting and lonely tasks a person can be given. Carers grieve for someone who is still alive, sometimes for years, a loss with no funeral. They lose sleep, friends and often their own health. Many are quietly depressed.

Scripture calls us to honour our parents (Exodus 20:12) and to provide for our own family: “if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith” (1 Timothy 5:8). But to honour and provide does not always mean caring for them at home yourself. There comes a point for many families when good residential care is the most loving and responsible choice. Help carers make that decision without guilt, and keep visiting after the move.

For a spouse, the vow was “in sickness and in health.” Robertson McQuilkin’s decision to leave his post and care for his wife Muriel has encouraged many. But not every spouse can do what he did, and the church should not lay that weight on anyone who is already breaking. The church shares the load: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).

What the church can do

Arrange a rota so the carer can have a few free hours each week, for rest, for church, or simply for a walk. Offer transport to appointments. Ask the carer how they are, not only how the patient is. Make your services welcoming to people with dementia, with familiar hymns and patience with interruptions. And if the person becomes aggressive, wanders, or behaves in ways that embarrass the family, respond with understanding, not shame, and help the family seek medical advice.

The end of the story

Dementia is part of the curse, and it is not the end. The body that is slowly failing will be raised: “It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power” (1 Corinthians 15:43). The mind that is clouded will be made clear in the presence of Christ. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). On that day, she will remember everything that matters, and she will know as she has been fully known (1 Corinthians 13:12). We serve her now as people who believe that.

For reflection

Is there someone with dementia in your church or family whom you have stopped visiting? Who is caring for them, and what one practical thing could you do this week to share that carer’s load?

21.title: Recommended Literature and Resources
21.essay:
Biblical counselling has produced a rich body of literature over the past fifty years. Here is a counsellor’s library, arranged by topic. You do not need it all at once. Begin with the foundations, and add the rest as your ministry requires.

Foundations: start here

Paul David Tripp, Instruments in the Redeemer’s Hands (P&R, 2002), is the single most practical introduction. His four movements — love, know, speak, do — are accessible, pastoral and theologically sound. Read this first.

Heath Lambert, A Theology of Biblical Counseling (Zondervan, 2016), gives the most systematic theological foundation, showing how the doctrines of Scripture, humanity, sin, grace and sanctification ground the work of counselling. Essential for understanding the why behind the how.

David Powlison, Seeing with New Eyes (P&R, 2003), collects essays that show his heart-focused method at its best. His Speaking Truth in Love (New Growth Press) applies it practically.

Jay Adams, Competent to Counsel (1970), is the book that began the modern movement. Dated in places, but essential for understanding the tradition’s roots.

Timothy Lane and Paul Tripp, How People Change (New Growth Press, 2006), is the best introduction to how the gospel produces lasting change, and is excellent for counsellors and counselees alike.

The heart and the gospel

Brad Bigney, Gospel Treason: Betraying the Gospel with Hidden Idols (P&R, 2012), is the most accessible treatment of idols of the heart, and one every elder should read.

Tim Keller, Counterfeit Gods (2009), applies the diagnosis of idols to money, sex, power and approval with cultural sharpness and pastoral warmth.

Stuart Scott, From Pride to Humility (Focus Publishing, 2002), is a short, powerful treatment of pride as the root of much relational conflict. It pairs well with his The Exemplary Husband.

Common struggles

Edward Welch, Running Scared: Fear, Worry, and the God of Rest (New Growth Press, 2007), is perhaps the finest biblical treatment of anxiety. His Depression: A Stubborn Darkness (2004) is essential for depression, and Shame Interrupted (2012) for shame and abuse.

Edward Welch, Side by Side: Walking with Others in Wisdom and Love (Crossway, 2015), is the best introduction to everyday mutual care in the congregation: simple enough for any church member, rich enough for trained counsellors.

Martha Peace, The Excellent Wife (Focus Publishing), is a key text for counselling women in marriage, and her Damsels in Distress (P&R, 2006) addresses common struggles women face.

Amy Baker, Picture Perfect: When Life Doesn’t Line Up (New Growth Press, 2014), addresses perfectionism, expectations, and their link with eating disorders.

Steve Viars, Putting Your Past in Its Place (Harvest House, 2011), helps those whose past is controlling their present. His Loving Your Community describes a congregation-wide culture of care.

Hard cases

Heath Lambert, Finally Free: Fighting for Purity with the Power of Grace (Zondervan, 2013), is the best gospel-centred book on pornography for both counsellor and counselee.

Edward Welch, Addictions: A Banquet in the Grave (P&R, 2001), is the essential guide to addiction from a biblical perspective. His Blame It on the Brain? helps distinguish brain and heart in mental illness.

David Powlison, How Does Sanctification Work? (Crossway, 2017), is invaluable for understanding change in stubborn or slow situations.

John Street (editor), Men Counseling Men (Harvest House, 2013), is a comprehensive manual for the particular struggles men face.

Winston Smith, Marriage Matters (New Growth Press, 2010), is a helpful resource for marriage counselling.

John Swinton, Dementia: Living in the Memories of God (Eerdmans, 2012), is the deepest theological treatment of dementia and personhood. Benjamin Mast, Second Forgetting: Remembering the Power of the Gospel during Alzheimer’s Disease (Zondervan, 2014), is shorter and very practical for families. Robertson McQuilkin, A Promise Kept (Tyndale, 1998), is the moving story of a husband’s care for his wife.

Training and ongoing learning

The Association of Certified Biblical Counselors (ACBC) offers training, conferences and a network of certified counsellors. Certification involves study, examination and supervised counselling hours. The Christian Counseling and Educational Foundation (CCEF), co-founded by Jay Adams, is home to Edward Welch and the work of David Powlison, and its booklets, courses and Journal of Biblical Counseling are among the most useful materials available.

A reading plan

In your first year, read Tripp’s Instruments, Welch’s Side by Side, Bigney’s Gospel Treason and Powlison’s Seeing with New Eyes. Together they give you the foundation, the method, the diagnosis of the heart, and the pastoral posture. In your second year, add Lambert’s Theology of Biblical Counseling and Welch’s books on anxiety, depression and addictions. From then on, specialise according to the situations you meet most often, and try to attend at least one training event a year.

Supervised practice

Reading without supervised practice produces knowledgeable counsellors, but not necessarily effective ones. Find a more experienced biblical counsellor who will let you observe, then supervise your conversations, then debrief with you. The best counsellors always remain under some form of accountability, not because they are incompetent, but because the work is too important to do without it.

Tools, not substitutes

These books are not substitutes for theological depth, prayerful dependence and pastoral experience. They are tools for people already grounded in the word of God. Randy Patten’s vision for ACBC was a movement of counsellors embedded in local churches, enriching pastoral care rather than replacing it. The well-equipped congregation trains its pastors, elders and mature members, so that the whole body can be what Paul described: “full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another” (Romans 15:14).

For reflection

Which one book from this list will you begin with? Who could you ask to mentor you as you grow in caring for others?
